title: Fabric API for GraphQL: Sources to a Single Endpoint
purpose: Show how Fabric API for GraphQL turns connected data sources into an auto-generated schema and a single live endpoint — the portal setup workflow, what backends it supports, how schema evolution avoids versioned endpoints, and the human/AI-agent consumption paths on the other side.
accessibleSummary: An architecture diagram: connected data sources — Warehouse, SQL database, Lakehouse via its SQL analytics endpoint, Azure SQL Database, and Fabric mirrored databases — feed a portal-driven setup workflow where tables, views, and relationships are selected and modeled. Fabric auto-generates a GraphQL schema, resolvers, and a live endpoint from that configuration, with no custom backend code and no separate deployment step. The endpoint is queried by human application developers through an interactive portal editor and by AI agents through the Model Context Protocol. A built-in performance monitoring dashboard observes usage. A warning node covers schema evolution: Fabric favors additive, non-breaking changes over versioned v1/v2/v3 endpoints, and getting this wrong by treating GraphQL like a versioned REST API defeats the model's main advantage.
longDescription: This is an architecture diagram of Fabric API for GraphQL, tracing from connected data sources to consumption. It starts with the five documented supported source types, all reached through a SQL analytics endpoint of some kind, flowing into a portal-driven setup workflow (connect sources, choose tables/views/stored procedures, optionally model relationships, configure permissions). That configuration feeds automatic schema and resolver generation, producing a single live GraphQL endpoint with no deployment step. Two consumption paths fan out from the endpoint: the interactive portal editor for human developers testing queries, and an AI-agent path via the Model Context Protocol. A built-in performance monitoring dashboard observes the endpoint's usage. A warning node addresses schema evolution directly, because it is the one place a team can accidentally reintroduce the REST versioning problem GraphQL's field-selection model was meant to avoid.

nodes.label: Connected data sources
nodes.summary: Warehouse, SQL database, Lakehouse, Azure SQL Database, and mirrored databases — all reached through a SQL analytics endpoint.
nodes.detail: Supported data sources for the GraphQL API include Fabric Data Warehouse, Fabric SQL database, Fabric Lakehouse (via its SQL analytics endpoint), Azure SQL Database, and Fabric mirrored databases (including Azure SQL DB, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Cosmos DB, Fabric SQL Database, Azure Databricks, Snowflake, and open mirrored databases) accessed through their SQL analytics endpoints.
nodes.whyItMatters: The common thread across every supported source is that it routes through a SQL analytics endpoint — this is what lets one GraphQL item generate a consistent schema and resolver layer regardless of which of Fabric's item types is actually attached.

evidence.note: Supported data sources for the GraphQL API include Fabric Data Warehouse, Fabric SQL database, Fabric Lakehouse (via its SQL analytics endpoint), Azure SQL Database, and Fabric mirrored databases (including Azure SQL DB, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Cosmos DB, Fabric SQL Database, Azure Databricks, Snowflake, and open mirrored databases) accessed through their SQL analytics endpoints.

inputs: Data already landed in a Fabric Warehouse, SQL database, Lakehouse, Azure SQL Database, or mirrored database
processing: No transformation at this node — represents the eligible source estate as-is
Each source is reached via its SQL analytics endpoint rather than a source-specific driver
outputs: A pool of connectable sources available to a GraphQL item during setup
drill.example: A team has customer data in a Warehouse and order data in a mirrored Azure SQL Database; both are eligible GraphQL sources because both expose a SQL analytics endpoint.
controls: Which sources exist and are network-reachable to the GraphQL item's setup workflow
failureModes: Assuming an unsupported source type (e.g. a raw Lakehouse Files folder with no Delta table) can be connected directly

nodes.label: Portal setup workflow
nodes.summary: Create the item, connect sources, choose what to expose, model relationships, configure permissions — no deployment step.
nodes.detail: Setting up a GraphQL item in Fabric is a portal-driven workflow: create the item, connect data sources, choose which tables/views/stored procedures to expose, optionally model relationships, and configure access permissions, after which the endpoint is immediately queryable with no separate deployment step.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is what makes GraphQL API a configuration-driven access layer rather than a service teams have to build, package, and deploy — the moment configuration finishes, the endpoint exists.

evidence.note: Setting up a GraphQL item in Fabric is a portal-driven workflow: create the item, connect data sources, choose which tables/views/stored procedures to expose, optionally model relationships, and configure access permissions, after which the endpoint is immediately queryable with no separate deployment step.

inputs: The pool of connectable Fabric/Azure sources
Decisions about which tables/views/stored procedures to expose
processing: Create the GraphQL item
Connect one or more data sources
Choose exposed tables, views, or stored procedures
Optionally model one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many relationships between them
Configure access permissions
outputs: A fully configured GraphQL item, ready for schema generation
drill.example: A developer connects a Warehouse's Customers table and a mirrored database's Orders table, models a one-to-many Customer-to-Orders relationship, and sets read permissions for the application's service principal — all inside the portal, no code written.
controls: Which tables/views/procedures are exposed (narrower is safer than exposing everything by default)
failureModes: Exposing every table in a connected source by default instead of deliberately selecting the minimal set an application actually needs

nodes.label: Auto-generated schema, resolvers, endpoint
nodes.summary: No custom backend code — the schema, resolvers, and live endpoint are all generated from the setup configuration.
nodes.detail: Fabric API for GraphQL automatically generates a GraphQL schema, resolvers, and a live endpoint from connected data sources, so no custom backend code is required to expose the data. GraphQL items support fan-out queries across multiple attached data sources and can model one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships between exposed entities.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the architectural core of the product: the item you create isn't a shell to fill in with resolver logic — it's the finished artifact once sources, exposed tables, relationships, and permissions are configured.

evidence.note: Fabric API for GraphQL automatically generates a GraphQL schema, resolvers, and a live endpoint from connected data sources, so no custom backend code is required to expose the data.
GraphQL items support fan-out queries across multiple attached data sources and can model one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships between exposed entities.

inputs: The configured GraphQL item: exposed tables/views/procedures, modeled relationships, permissions
processing: Generate a GraphQL schema (types and fields) from the exposed tables/views
Generate resolvers that fan out across attached sources following the modeled relationships
Publish the schema and resolvers as a live endpoint
outputs: A queryable GraphQL schema and a live endpoint URL, with no service deployed by the team
drill.example: The Customer/Orders configuration from the setup step generates a schema where a Customer type has an orders field that fans out, at query time, to the mirrored database via the modeled relationship.
controls: The exposed tables/views/relationships from setup are the only inputs this step has — no separate resolver customization
failureModes: Expecting to hand-write custom resolver logic the way a typical GraphQL server allows — Fabric's is generated, not user-authored

nodes.label: Field-selection query model
nodes.summary: A client names only the fields and relationships it needs, in one round trip — no over-fetching, no N+1.
nodes.detail: The API for GraphQL is built so a single query can request only the specific fields a client needs and traverse defined relationships in one round trip, avoiding both over-fetching and the N+1 query pattern common to REST.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the client-facing payoff of the whole architecture: a mobile app that only needs a customer's name and their last three orders makes one call instead of a cascade of follow-up calls per related record.

evidence.note: The API for GraphQL is built so a single query can request only the specific fields a client needs and traverse defined relationships in one round trip, avoiding both over-fetching and the N+1 query pattern common to REST.

inputs: A client-issued GraphQL query naming specific fields and relationship traversals
processing: Parse the query against the generated schema
Resolve only the named fields and relationships, fanning out to underlying sources as needed
Assemble a single typed JSON response
outputs: One response payload shaped exactly like the client's query, in one round trip
drill.example: A mobile app requests { customer(id: X) { name orders(last: 3) { placedAt total } } } and gets back exactly those fields in one call, instead of a REST GET for the customer plus three follow-up GETs per order.
controls: What fields and relationships the client chooses to request — the model naturally scopes cost to actual need
failureModes: A poorly modeled deep relationship chain letting a client's single query fan out to an unexpectedly large number of underlying source calls

nodes.label: Interactive portal editor
nodes.summary: Human developers build and test queries in-browser with a results pane, parameterized queries, and Intellisense.
nodes.detail: The GraphQL API includes an interactive editor in the Fabric portal with a results pane, parameterized query/mutation support, and schema-aware Intellisense for building and testing queries.
nodes.whyItMatters: This gives an application developer a way to iterate on and validate a query against the live schema before writing any client-side integration code.

evidence.note: The GraphQL API includes an interactive editor in the Fabric portal with a results pane, parameterized query/mutation support, and schema-aware Intellisense for building and testing queries.

processing: Offer schema-aware Intellisense as a developer types a query
Execute parameterized queries or mutations against the live endpoint
Render results in an in-portal results pane
outputs: A validated query a developer can copy directly into an application
drill.example: A developer drafts the RecentOrders query shape in the portal editor, sees the actual JSON response in the results pane, then pastes the finished query into their mobile app's GraphQL client.
controls: Which permissions the developer's own identity has when testing in the editor
failureModes: Testing successfully in the editor under a privileged identity, then discovering a production caller's narrower permissions can't reach the same fields

nodes.label: AI-agent access via MCP
nodes.summary: AI agents connect to the same endpoint through the Model Context Protocol, not only human application developers.
nodes.detail: Microsoft now documents a path to connect AI agents to Fabric data through the GraphQL endpoint using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), positioning the API as an agent-facing data access layer in addition to a human application API.
nodes.whyItMatters: The same schema-and-resolver layer built for a mobile app's data needs is also the interface an AI agent uses to reach into Warehouse, Lakehouse, or mirrored-database data — one modeled item can plausibly serve both audiences without duplicating access logic.

evidence.note: Microsoft now documents a path to connect AI agents to Fabric data through the GraphQL endpoint using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), positioning the API as an agent-facing data access layer in addition to a human application API.

inputs: The live GraphQL endpoint and its schema
An AI agent framework speaking MCP
processing: Agent connects to the GraphQL endpoint as an MCP tool
Agent issues field-scoped GraphQL queries the same way a human-facing client would
outputs: Structured, typed data returned to the agent for reasoning or response generation
drill.example: An AI agent answering a support question calls the same GraphQL endpoint a mobile app uses, requesting only the customer and order fields relevant to the question via MCP.
controls: Access permissions configured on the GraphQL item apply identically to MCP callers as to human-facing clients
failureModes: Exposing a broader, unshaped schema to an agent than would be given to a deliberately scoped human-facing application

nodes.label: Performance monitoring dashboard
nodes.summary: Built-in request logging tracks endpoint usage and behavior over time.
nodes.detail: Fabric exposes a built-in performance monitoring dashboard with request logging for GraphQL API items, intended to track API usage and behavior over time.
nodes.whyItMatters: This gives a platform team visibility into how an endpoint is actually being used and behaving in production without instrumenting a custom logging service themselves.

evidence.note: Fabric exposes a built-in performance monitoring dashboard with request logging for GraphQL API items, intended to track API usage and behavior over time.

inputs: Requests flowing through the live GraphQL endpoint, from both human clients and AI agents
processing: Log each request
Aggregate usage and behavior into the performance monitoring dashboard
outputs: Visibility into query patterns and endpoint behavior over time, without a custom-built observability layer
drill.example: A platform team notices via the dashboard that a specific deeply-nested query pattern from the mobile app is issued far more often than expected, prompting a review of the client's query design.
controls: No configuration required — this is a built-in capability of any GraphQL API item
failureModes: Relying on this dashboard alone for quantified latency or throughput numbers, which it does not provide — see the performance-characteristics gap noted in the article

nodes.label: Anti-pattern: versioned endpoints (v1/v2/v3)
nodes.summary: Fabric's schema evolution favors additive change and deprecation — minting versioned endpoints defeats the model's advantage.
nodes.detail: Fabric's GraphQL schema evolution favors additive, non-breaking changes and field deprecation over issuing versioned endpoints (v1/v2/v3), since clients only receive fields they explicitly request.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because clients only ever receive the fields they explicitly request, a new field cannot break an existing client that never queries it — reaching for a versioned endpoint on every schema change reintroduces exactly the migration overhead GraphQL's request-what-you-need shape was meant to avoid.

evidence.note: Fabric's GraphQL schema evolution favors additive, non-breaking changes and field deprecation over issuing versioned endpoints (v1/v2/v3), since clients only receive fields they explicitly request.

inputs: A schema change request — for example, adding a new field or renaming an existing one
processing: Correct approach: add the new field alongside the old one, mark the old field @deprecated with a reason
Anti-pattern: stand up a new versioned endpoint (/graphql/v2) and require all clients to migrate wholesale
outputs: Correct approach: existing clients keep working unmodified; new clients opt into the new field when ready
Anti-pattern: every client, including ones that never needed the change, must migrate on a forced timeline
drill.example: A team adds loyaltyTierV2 alongside the existing loyaltyTier field and deprecates the old one with a reason string; a mobile app querying only { name orders { ... } } is entirely unaffected by the change.
controls: Discipline to design new fields as additive and use field deprecation instead of reaching for a new endpoint version
failureModes: A team used to REST versioning habits reflexively minting v2/v3 GraphQL endpoints, splitting the client base and losing the additive-change advantage entirely

edges.label: queried by AI agents via MCP
risk if evolved via versioned endpoints instead of additive fields

walkthrough.title: Start: five source types, one common thread
walkthrough.explanation: Warehouse, SQL database, Lakehouse, Azure SQL Database, and mirrored databases are all reached through a SQL analytics endpoint, which is what lets one generation layer serve them all.

walkthrough.title: Configuration, not deployment
walkthrough.explanation: Connecting sources, exposing tables, modeling relationships, and setting permissions is entirely portal-driven — there is no build-and-deploy cycle.

walkthrough.title: The schema and resolvers are generated, not written
walkthrough.explanation: This is the architectural core: the finished GraphQL item is the output of configuration, with no custom backend code required.

walkthrough.title: One round trip, exactly the fields needed
walkthrough.explanation: The field-selection query model is what avoids both over-fetching and the N+1 pattern common to REST.

walkthrough.title: Human developers test in the portal
walkthrough.explanation: The in-portal editor with Intellisense and a results pane lets a developer validate a query against the live schema before writing client code.

walkthrough.title: AI agents reach the same endpoint via MCP
walkthrough.explanation: The same schema-and-resolver layer is positioned as an agent-facing data access surface, not only a human application API.

walkthrough.title: Usage is observable out of the box
walkthrough.explanation: A built-in dashboard with request logging tracks how the endpoint is actually used, without a custom-built observability layer.

walkthrough.title: Warning: don't reach for versioned endpoints
walkthrough.explanation: Fabric's schema evolution model is built around additive change; minting v1/v2/v3 endpoints on every change defeats the field-selection model's main advantage.
